entries.title: At odds over the EU budget, European leaders cut summit short - DW has more
entries.summary: Even before they met, it was clear the gap between European leaders' demands for the EU budget would make negotiations difficult. They ended a summit meeting early and aim to agree on EU funding in December. DW has more.
entries.content:
Europe

At odds over budget, EU leaders break off summit early

Published November 26, 2026last updated November 27, 2026

Even before they met, it was clear the gap between European leaders' demands for the EU budget would make negotiations difficult. They ended a summit meeting early and aim to agree on EU funding in December. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Special European Council meeting ends early after leaders disagree on budget
  • Details of long-term budget, Ukraine's 2027 financial needs and ECB leadership were on the agenda
  • Spaniard Pablo Hernandez de Cos to take over as head of the ECB

You can follow developments from the EU summit taking place on Thursday, November 26, below:

Skip next section Antonia Costa wraps up EU summit that fails to close gaps in budget disputes

Antonia Costa wraps up EU summit that fails to close gaps in budget disputes

European Council President Antonio Costa said that 24 out of 27 members of the EU supported a proposal for a €45 billion loan for Ukraine.

That loan is split into two sections, with €20 billion to help finance for civil services and the other €25 billion going to arms and ammunition.

Euro News reported earlier in the day that Bulgaria reversed course and was ready to join the loan, so long as it was only paying into the part that wasn't covering Ukraine's military needs.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said there was considerable work to be done before a deal could be in place.

EU leaders cut short a second day of talks that was due to take place tomorrow and pushed discussions to another summit in December.

The disagreements over a shared EU budget for the years between 2028 and 2034 stem from different priorities among EU members.

Some countries prefer greater funding for defense and enhancing competitiveness, while others seek to keep in place funding for agriculture, among other issues.

EU leaders ultimately weren't able to reach an agreement at the end of Thursday.

Skip next section Macron says Le Pen was 'arrogant' in speaking as if she was president already

Macron says Le Pen was 'arrogant' in speaking as if she was president already

French President Emmanuel Macron said far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen should be more humble after she criticized efforts to reach a deal on the EU budget before the end of the year.

EU leaders were gathered in Brussels throughout the day to see if they could hammer out an agreement over a shared budget from 2028 to 2034.

But they remain far apart on many issues, including some members opposing the use of funds for military aid to Ukraine.

During the day, Le Pen, who is projected to beat her centrist rivals in the April 2027 elections, accused Macron and the European Commission of trying to rush through a budget deal before next year.

"The apparent aim is to ‌deter ​us from defending France's interests in EU budget negotiations if the French people entrust us with the responsibility of governing," she said in a post on X.

Macron hit back, saying later: "Mrs. Le Pen is campaigning. It takes a peculiar kind ​of arrogance to think she’s already in charge ​of France's destiny. ‌Last I checked, she wasn’t elected."

Macron said he was careful to take into account the presidential election and that if there was no deal by December 31, negotiations would have to resume in the second half of 2027, when his successor would be in office.

"You have to be more humble when you're campaigning, even if you already see yourself in the job," Macron said.

Skip next section No progress yet in EU budget talks, Dutch PM Rob Jetten says

No progress yet in EU budget talks, Dutch PM Rob Jetten says

EU leaders hadn't made as much progress in their discussions about the EU's next long-term budget, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said.

Jetten said it was up to EU Council President Antonio Costa to come up with an improvised proposal for the next budget, which he said would be debated in "more intense" negotiations in December.

EU leaders are still hoping to have another round of talks around midnight before calling it a day.

Like Germany, the Netherlands is a net contributor to the European Union.

Skip next section EU budget talks delayed until December summit, Merz says

EU budget talks delayed until December summit, Merz says

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said EU leaders will try to reach an agreement on the next multi-annual budget for the EU by the end of this year.

Merz said a day of talks among EU leaders in Brussels had brought "new movement" toward a reduction of the proposed size of the next budget, as demanded by Germany and other countries that are net contributors to the bloc's finances.

The leaders will try to hammer out a deal during a two-day summit starting December 17, Merz said.

Germany has been leading calls to attach a durable funding scheme for Ukraine to the EU's next budget.

Merz has made clear that his country would approve the next budget if all countries backed a loan for Ukraine.

Last year, the EU reached an agreement on a €90 billion loan to Ukraine through a compromise loan after a much-discussed frozen-asset plan failed.

The Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia opted out of backing the loan.

Skip next section EU leaders to meet later tonight, Merz says

EU leaders to meet later tonight, Merz says

Contrary to earlier expectations, European Union leaders weren't quite done for the day, even if it was well past 2200 local time.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that rather than meet again as scheduled on Friday, leaders would hold a final round of discussions around midnight and end the summit.

Skip next section Thank you for following our coverage

Thank you for following our coverage

Thank you for reading along with our coverage of the Euro Summit on Thursday.

We will be back tomorrow to bring you the latest from the second day.

Until then, you can watch DW's analysis of the event:

Skip next section Hungary's Magyar sees 'virtually zero chance' of reaching a deal on Thursday

Hungary's Magyar sees 'virtually zero chance' of reaching a deal on Thursday

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has said the chances of reaching an agreement on Thursday are "virtually zero."

Leaders of the European Union are gathered today in Brussels to agree on the bloc's budget proposal for 2028 to 2034.

In an X post, Magyar said he outlined "Hungary’s priorities and the red lines" to the other member states.

"Having heard the completely opposing positions around the table, I would put the chances of reaching an agreement today at virtually zero," he wrote.

He also said "an agreement around Christmas looks unlikely" as well.

Skip next section Pedro Sanchez welcomes nomination of Hernandez de Cos as new ECB chief

Pedro Sanchez welcomes nomination of Hernandez de Cos as new ECB chief

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez celebrated "a Spain that leads in Europe like never before," after the nomination of Pablo Hernandez de Cos as the next European Central Bank (ECB) chief.

Hernandez de Cos is set to become the new ECB head as the European Union (EU) leaders are gathered in Brussels for the Euro Summit.

Sanchez welcomed the news in a post on X, pointing out that the top EU positions held by Spanish officials Teresa Ribera, the European Commission's First Executive Vice-President, and Nadia Calvino, head of the European Investment Bank.

"In short, Spain leads in Europe like never before," he wrote.

Skip next section Pablo Hernandez de Cos is set to become the new European Central Bank chief — reports

Pablo Hernandez de Cos is set to become the new European Central Bank chief — reports

Spanish candidate Pablo Hernandez de Cos will become the next president of the European Central Bank (ECB), after being endorsed by the majority ‌of ​eurozone countries, news agencies reported.

As the leaders gather for the Euro Summit, the Financial Times first reported that de Cos will be the next ECB chief, citing ​people ​familiar with ​the matter. This was confirmed by Reuters and AFP, citing EU diplomat sources.

The decision came after the Netherlands said it would support the Spaniard as a consensus candidate.

Christine Lagarde has been president since November 2019 but has announced her intention to step down on February 7, 2027.

De Cos was up against Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot for the presidency, while France's Laurence Boone and Germany's Markus Brunnermeier have been nominated for the ECB's two other top jobs.

Skip next section Russia says EU budget plans would prolong war in Ukraine

Russia says EU budget plans would prolong war in Ukraine

Russia has criticized the European Union's proposed seven-year budget, accusing the bloc of seeking to prolong the war in Ukraine.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the EU's plans to allocate money for Ukraine in its budget would make Kyiv "less inclined toward a peace process and more determined to continue the war."

Peskov said the result would be more military spending, leaving less for governments to spend on school, hospitals and social facilities.

"This is not money for peace," Peskov said.

Support for Ukraine is among the key areas of discussion in the 2028-2034 budget which includes up to €100 billion for Ukraine, however diplomats say this figure falls well short of Kyiv's needs.

Skip next section EU 'light-years' from budget deal, Italy PM Meloni says

EU 'light-years' from budget deal, Italy PM Meloni says

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has added her voice to those warning that European leaders have their work cut out for them when it comes to agreeing on a multi-year budget proposal.

"We're light-years ‌away from a ‌solution," ​Meloni told reporters ahead of the EU summit in Brussels.

"We are not willing ⁠to ​sign off ​on a budget ​under which ‌we would have to ​give ⁠more to receive less," ⁠she ​added.

Earlier, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the budget was "still too high" and that members states needed to be able to afford the full cost without taking on new debt.

Last week, European Council President Antonio Costa presented a new compromise proposal of €1.78 trillion ($1.95 trillion), around €204 billion lower than the initial proposal by the European Commission.

Skip next section Analysis: The battle for Europe's future behind closed doors

Analysis: The battle for Europe's future behind closed doors

Every seven years, European leaders gather in Brussels for what is arguably the most consequential negotiation cycle in the European Union. As German Chancellor Friedrich Merz put it upon arrival, it is about "the future of the European Union."

This is not a typical EU summit. The leaders of the 27 member states are confronting a question that will shape all angles of EU politics for years to come: How much money should the EU have, who should pay for it, and what should it be spent on?

It is the essence of EU summit diplomacy: a painstaking exercise in give-and-take, bargaining and compromise.

The European Commission laid down the opening bid over the summer. The proposal was ambitious. Brussels wants an EU budget that reflects a rapidly-changing world: more spending on defence, innovation, research, digital technologies and competitiveness. At the same time, that inevitably means pressure on some of the traditional pillars of EU spending, particularly agricultural subsidies and parts of the bloc's regional development programmes.

Since then, every member has arrived with a shopping list of demands.

Governments have pushed back against cuts, demanded new priorities, sought exemptions and fought for national interests. There have though also been others who are pushing FOR a reduction in spending, including Merz.

The original proposal from Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has already undergone numerous adjustments as negotiators attempted to accommodate competing demands.

The result is an extraordinarily complex puzzle.

At the centre of it all stands European Council President Antonio Costa. He will be shuttling between bilateral meetings with leaders, gather small groups behind closed doors and attempt to construct a package that gives everybody something they can take home and present as a victory.

For Costa, the stakes are high. Delivering an agreement would be a major test of his authority and reputation as the EU's chief broker. Especially as he was not made top negotiator for the EU in the peace talks on Russia's war in Ukraine. Diplomats expressed confidence in his fairness and negotiating skills before the summit, viewing him as someone capable of building trust among leaders who have differing priorities.

Yet nobody in Brussels expects an easy breakthrough. Many officials acknowledge that the pressure on member states may not yet be intense enough to force the final concessions required for a deal. Leaders are still defending red lines rather than crossing them.

So, this summit will highly likely end without a grand agreement. Leaders will probably decide to take stock of the latest negotiating proposals and return home to assess them in detail. There will be a new — and perhaps final — round on the next summit in December, a few days before Christmas.

Skip next section WATCH: Is Gen Z really worse off than their parents?

WATCH: Is Gen Z really worse off than their parents?

As leaders grapple with long-term budgets, across Europe, young people are rising up. They're demanding better jobs, more funding for education and lower rents. The problems they are protesting are complex and often specific to their home country.

But there’s also a common message: Young people feel pessimistic about their economic future. A look at the data shows they could be right.

Skip next section Bulgaria ready to back non-military aid for Ukraine

Bulgaria ready to back non-military aid for Ukraine

Bulgaria's Prime Minister Rumen Radev said his country would support a proposed €45 billion ($49 billion) EU loan to Ukraine, but only the funds earmarked for non-military aid.

"Bulgaria is going to take part ​in the loan of €20 billion (for) non-military support for Ukraine," ⁠Radev ​told reporters as he arrived ​at the EU summit in Brussels.

"We ​have a ‌huge historic diaspora of Bulgarians living in Ukraine, our wish ​is ⁠to concentrate our support in that area. ⁠We are ​going to contribute, but no money from Bulgaria for weapons," Radev said.

Last week European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the €45 billion would be split into two parts: ‌up to €25 billion for military aid and up to €20 billion for other ‌help as a means of getting member states to contribute where there were objections to funding weapons for Ukraine.

Skip next section Germany's Merz says EU budget proposal 'still too high'

Germany's Merz says EU budget proposal 'still too high'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that the budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 was "still too too high" and did not provide the basis for an agreement, during comments made as he arrived at the summit.

"After all, the member states must be able ​to afford to pay for ⁠all ​of this," Merz said in Brussels.

​The German leader also said the war in Ukraine needed to be ended as soon as possible and that the country needed help during a "very difficult winter."

Merz said that funding for Kyiv is "a task that we must also accomplish together,” and added: "The European Union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."

Slovakia, the Czech Republic, and Hungary have been exempt from contributing to aid for Ukraine. The countries negotiated, as part of the current €90 billion loan for Ukraine, that they would not have financial obligations in guaranteeing the loan.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis did not agree with the German chancellor.

"Funding for Ukraine should be negotiated separately," said Babis, adding that his country needs the money for other expenditures. "I believe we will fight for this money," providing an early indication of how talks might proceed over the next two days.

entries.title: Albania's youth are protesting in Flamingo Revolution, not leaving the country anymore
entries.summary: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.
entries.content:
Albania

Albania's youth are protesting, not leaving the country anymore

November 26, 2026

Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.

In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.

For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.

It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property. 

'Flamingo revolution' has broad support

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.

Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

Alternating between Socialist and Democratic Party

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."

Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."

It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."

The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.

Protesters call out corruption, face high cost of living

Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.

Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.

Albanians largely pro-EU

Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.

Though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.

What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.

Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Gerard Depardieu to stand trial in France for rape and sexual assault
entries.summary: The Paris Court of Appeal upheld the order for the 77-year-old French actor to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in 2018.
entries.content:
November 26, 2026

The Paris Court of Appeal upheld the order for the 77-year-old French actor to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in 2018.

French actor Gerard Depardieu failed in his attempt to overturn an order for him to stand trial on rape charges.

On Thursday, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that Depardieu should face trial for the alleged rape and sexual assault that occurred on August 7, 2018. However, the court dismissed the allegations relating to a second incident that occurred six days later.

Depardieu still has the option of appealing to a higher court. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told the Associated Press that she disputes Thursday's ruling, though she did not specify whether she will challenge it in France's highest civil and criminal court.

This decision comes just two weeks after the 77-year-old Depardieu dropped his appeal against a sexual assault conviction in a separate case. He accepted an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issued a public apology.

What are the charges against Depardieu?

An actress, who was 22 years old at the time, accused Depardieu of raping and sexually assaulting her at his Paris apartment on August 7 and 13, 2018. Depardieu was 69 at the time of the alleged incident.

She reported the allegations to the police a few days later. Depardieu denies the allegations, claiming that the encounter was consensual.

Last year, a trial was ordered regarding the allegations. If the trial goes ahead, Depardieu could face up to 20 years in prison.

Carine Durrieu Diebolt, the victim's lawyer, said that the Thursday decision was a genuine relief and a victory for her client.

Accusations overshadow Depardieu's legacy

Depardieu was born in 1948 into a working-class family in Chateauroux, a city in central France. He overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors.

The film star was a dominant figure in French cinema for half a century, becoming a renowned cultural export. He earned an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."

Accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction, however, have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

The international media has also been paying attention to Depardieu's off-screen antics. One of the most notable instances was when he accepted a Russian passport from President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

entries.title: Guinea-Bissau junta delays presidential vote for 2 years
entries.summary: The decision came exactly one year after the military took power on November 26, 2025. The junta said the conditions were insufficient to hold presidential elections for now.
entries.content:
Guinea-Bissau

Guinea-Bissau junta delays presidential vote for 2 years

November 26, 2026

The decision came exactly one year after the military took power on November 26, 2025. The junta said the conditions were insufficient to hold presidential elections for now.

The ruling junta in the West African nation of Guinea-Bissau announced Thursday that it is postponing elections by two years until November 26, 2028.

What do we know so far?

The decision came on the 1-year anniversary of the military takeover in Guinea-Bissau on November 26, 2025. The country is currently led by military general Horta Inta-a, who serves as transitional president.

Inta-a said in a statement that there was "an insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the election.

"It is essential to guarantee effective conditions for preparing and holding elections in accordance with the principles of legality, democratic participation, equal opportunity, transparency and electoral integrity," he said.

The military coup in Guinea-Bissau came three days after a general election last year, with the military deposing incumbent President Umaro Sissoco Embalo. Both Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias da Costa claimed victory in the election, with the military arresting Embalo one day prior to the results being released.

What's the political and human rights situation in Guinea-Bissau?

West African bloc ECOWAS has urged Guinea-Bissau to transition back to civilian rule. 

Guinea-Bissau is a small tropical Portuguese-speaking nation on the West African coast which has seen multiple coups in its history. The country faces a high level of corruption and is also a key point for cocaine trafficking to Europe.

According to Washington DC-based think tank Freedom House, Guinea-Bissau is only "partly free" due to military interference in elections.

Reporters without Borders ranksGuinea-Bissau 100 out of 180 countries on its press freedom index, saying the "sharp deterioration of security for media professionals, combined with political and economic pressure, has severely tested the practice of journalism in recent years."

entries.title: Trial of Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia begins after delay
entries.summary: Despite delays due to health issues, the trial of the Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia has begun. Prosecutors say the defendant used her military contacts to provide information on German defense and Ukraine.
entries.content:
Germany

Trial of Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia begins after delay

November 26, 2026

Despite delays due to health issues, the trial of the Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia has begun. Prosecutors say the defendant used her military contacts to provide information on German defense and Ukraine.

The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman on charges of spying for Russia started Thursday.

The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.

Later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses. Her lawyers caused further delay when they said she would not confirm her personal information.

Several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys said their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.

Espionage process with diplomatic fallout

The arrest of the 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman triggered a diplomatic clash between Berlin and Moscow.

The Russian ambassador was summoned regarding the incident, and Andrei Mayerov, the deputy military attache at the embassy, was expelled from Germany.

Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power.

Her full name has not been released due to German privacy laws. She was arrested on January 21 and put in pretrial detention.

The trial is expected to last until May 2027.

What is Ilona W. accused of?

She is accused of having contacts with current and former German Defense Ministry officials to provide information about defense industry locations, drone tests and planned drone deliveries to Ukraine.

She was also said to have been in contact with a man, her alleged handler, working for Russian intelligence at the Russian Embassy in Berlin since at least November 2023, prosecutors say.

On several occasions, she allegedly helped her contact at the embassy attend political events in Berlin under a false identity in order to establish contacts there. She is also suspected of having compiled background information on participants in high-level political events.

Berlin summoned the alleged handler, who was identified by Der Spiegel magazine as the embassy's deputy military attache, over the incident and expelled him from Germany.

Ilona W. led an advocacy group for years that called for international cooperation, focusing particularly on German, Russian, Ukrainian relations.

In addition to her advocacy work, she also ran a small marketing agency.

Both positions allowed her to be active in Berlin's political circles and provided her with connections within the military.

Russia rejects the allegations

The Russian ambassador to Berlin, Sergei Nechayev, denied the allegations this week.

"The Russian Embassy has no connection whatsoever to this woman, and even if she happened to cross paths with one of our representatives, perhaps at some reception, that means absolutely nothing," Nechayev told news agency AFP.

He also said "he may have seen her himself at an event."

"But she is not a Russian citizen and, as far as we are aware, has no ties to Russia. She is a German and Ukrainian citizen, and, frankly, we do not associate with such individuals here," he said.

entries.title: Saudi pop music is thriving — but for the right reasons?
entries.summary: As part of Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's music scene has evolved hugely thanks to state funding and support. Local musicians and DJs are optimistic. But are they actually just helping prop up an authoritarian state?
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Saudi pop music is thriving — but for the right reasons?

November 26, 2026

As part of Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's music scene has evolved hugely thanks to state funding and support. Local musicians and DJs are optimistic. But are they actually just helping prop up an authoritarian state?

Today, rapper Asayel Bishi is one of Saudi Arabia's rising hip-hop stars, signed to the country's biggest record label for new music, MDLBEAST. But not so long ago, she was making international headlines for a totally different reason.

In 2020, after Bishi released a music video for a song, "Bint Mecca," or "girl from Mecca," featuring people dancing in a local cafe, Mecca's governor called for the arrest of Bishi's whole production team. He said the video violated the holy city's local customs and traditions. In the end, the situation was resolved with a discussion about filming permits.

And by early 2023, Bishi was signed to MDLBEAST and has since racked up hundreds of thousands of streams on music platforms like Spotify.

In the past, other Saudi rappers have ended up in prison for similar, alleged transgressions. The fact that Bishi's story went a different way is probably partially because the 31-year-old's career path is on a similar trajectory to the Saudi pop music industry as a whole.

Music part of Vision 2030

As part of Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 plan, announced in 2016 and which aims to move the country away from economic dependence on oil, the country has poured billions into the local music industry.

The pace of development increased in 2019 after the country held its first major festival, Soundstorm, an annual event that now draws major international acts and over 400,000 guests. MDLBEAST was created then, primarily as the festival organizer. Since then, it has also become a record label, radio station, distributor, promoter and talent incubator.

A recent report for the Saudi Music Commission suggests the music sector could be worth $500 million (€455 million) by 2034. But it's difficult to figure out how well Saudi pop is really doing now because independent monitoring of the sector only began relatively recently.

Streaming platform Spotify reports that people listening to Saudi-made music inside Saudi Arabia increased by 195% between 2020 and 2024. However, the most-streamed artists inside the country are still international.

'Tied to the destiny of crown prince'

Although there was a mostly-hidden Saudi music scene before this recent boom, observers say the growth of the Saudi music sector is not organic.

It's all about building an industry from the top down, Amr Abdelrahim, a researcher at Sciences Po in Paris, reported in a 2024 study. "After 2016, young middle-class musicians and creative professionals, who had been careful to avoid drawing official attention to their countercultural activities suddenly became central to the ambitions of the state," he wrote.

The careers of young Saudi acts — like Bishi, for example — "became tied to the destiny of the crown prince," the researcher explained.

The Saudi royal family has long dispersed money from Saudi oil sales to their subjects, in order to ensure economic dependence and loyalty. But, Abdelrahim argued, "what is new about Saudi investments in culture under MBS is an unprecedented degree of centralization and the emergence of new clientelist networks around the country's de-facto ruler," using a common abbreviation for Crown Prince Mohammed.

Those involved "are inadvertently participating in the consolidation of the Saudi regime," he argued.

Observers say a lot of the new music businesses are vague about their ties to the state. But it's clear they couldn't work without the state's financial support and approval.

"Almost all major events are organized by the state or funded by closely linked entities," a spokesperson from Saudi-focused organization, ALQST for Human Rights, told DW. "This affects the type of music produced, as musicians have to be mindful of what is acceptable. This is not just about the music they produce, but also how they act and what they say to their fans."

ALQST believes Saudi musicians have even less artistic freedom under the new musical system than before, when they would have played or performed privately. They can lose their contracts and livelihoods, be prevented from performing or even arrested, ALQST's spokesperson said.

Hidden for two decades

"In the past, the music scene was not regulated," explained the guitarist and bassist for Saudi black metal band, Al-Namrood. But now that it is, the state can more closely monitor musicians who once stayed hidden and only played privately, the musician, who goes by the name of Mephisto, told DW.

Al-Namrood are one of the rare examples of a Saudi act that isn't working with state support. The group first formed in 2008 but have never played at home and have kept their identities secret for almost two decades.

"The exchange is clear: You want to perform, it has to be under our rules," Mephisto continued. "And I totally understand the perspective [of some musicians]. But typically the artist must refrain from any criticism of the religious or authoritarian. [The state] doesn't necessarily buy an artist's loyalty, it just creates incentives that make criticism increasingly costly."

For Al-Namrood, who have often condemned Saudi conservatism, religion and politics in their music, that's not an option. "We don't want anything to do with them," Mephisto said.

In her 2020 paper for the journal, Arabian Humanities, Nora Derbal, a professor at the University of Hamburg, said Saudi artists told her that if they got a call from authorities asking them to participate in a government project, it would be an offer they couldn't turn down.

The artists she spoke with were debating "their cooptation and loss of autonomy, and about the consequences for not joining in state projects," she wrote.

On the other hand, in various interviews, Saudi acts who have partaken in their country's pop music renaissance have also been positive: They don't have to hide anymore, they can play for larger audiences and they are paid. In an interview, one Saudi DJ described the first Soundstorm festival as like "Berlin after the fall of the wall" while others said they felt they were making history.

"So that's the interesting paradox," said Fannie Agerschou-Madsen, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Roskilde in Denmark, who's written several papers on the topic. "We have all these social liberalizations and challenges to conservative norms but at the same time that's not being followed by political liberalization."

Is the state co-opting local musicians?

But that doesn't mean that some room isn't being created for meaningful change, Agerschou-Madsen told DW. Locals told her they enjoyed the newfound freedom of going to a dance party although, she noted, the subversiveness seemed to be more directed at the social conservatism than Saudi authorities.

Young Saudis are well aware of the red lines and state control of the music scene and are continually negotiating boundaries, the researcher argued. In that way, "their everyday practices create space for political and social change, little by little, although perhaps not in what you'd consider a typically revolutionary way."

So is the Saudi state co-opting local musicians, including those who might have said something controversial before they ever get a chance to?

A DW enquiry to MDLBEAST was not answered. And the answer likely lies somewhere in the middle.

For some young Saudis, the new music scene has been about fun, self-expression, belonging and creativity, Agerschou-Madsen wrote in a new, as-yet-unpublished paper shared with DW. "Others, however, view it as a top-down project that commodifies fun while sidestepping deeper issues of political freedom and social equity."

entries.title: On farewell trip, Steinmeier calls for more investment in Africa
entries.summary: Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana, Kenya: On his last trip to Africa, outgoing German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier called on companies at home to be bolder and seize opportunities in Africa.
entries.content:
Germany

On farewell trip, Steinmeier calls for more investment in Africa

November 26, 2026

Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana, Kenya: On his last trip to Africa, outgoing German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier called on companies at home to be bolder and seize opportunities in Africa.

"My time as president is coming to an end, and that is why it was important to me to travel to Africa one more time — to the continent that is particularly close to my heart," said Frank-Walter Steinmeier during his final official trip to Africa. Over the course of 20 years, as president and before that as foreign minister, the veteran politician has made 30 trips to African countries.

"For me personally, things have come full circle today," the president added during his opening remarks at the German-African Business Summit in Ghana. He was alluding to the first German-African business summit in Berlin in 2015, which Steinmeier opened while he was still foreign minister in the administration of former Chancellor Angela Merkel.

This week, in addition to Ghana, he visited Cote d'Ivoire and Kenya with a business delegation from Germany.

Germany is competing — not just with China

A lot has happened since 2015, Steinmeier said. And yet: "We are still far from where we could be." Addressing Germany's business community, he said, "Be curious, take risks."

As the applause rang out after the speech, Jude Numfor, who works for the energy company REI in Cameroon, smiled. He too sees German companies as too risk-averse.

"When the Chinese come, they say 'let's do it,' and the Germans say 'let's prepare it'," he told DW.

Meanwhile, Africa's economy is growing rapidly. German-African foreign trade rose by 10.5% in 2025 to €63.4 billion ($69.4 billion). Africa's trade with the Asia-Pacific region is growing more slowly, but the absolute figures are also significantly higher.

This shows there is a great deal of potential in Africa's markets — especially in light of the emerging African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which encompasses most of the continent.

When it comes to direct investment, German companies are more hesitant than others — a trend observed not only by Numfor: China, Turkey and the Gulf states are willing to take on more risk and are pushing into these markets.

The Chinese, in particular, are offering large loans to build key rail lines and ports, and they are buying up mines and raw materials in Africa. But since they usually bring their own low-wage labor force with them, China's investments often create few local jobs.

Vocational training meant to open up new prospects

But such jobs would be the linchpin of Africa's future. In Kenya alone, 1 million young people enter the labor market each year; in Nigeria, the number is even higher, and some experts therefore anticipate even more irregular migration to Europe in the coming years.

Germany has said there is a need for action: It supports vocational training in Africa and, for several years now, has also been allowing skilled workers to emigrate to Germany from Africa.

During his trip, Steinmeier also visited educational institutions such as the vocational school for mechanics and industrial maintenance in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire. In Kenya, he spoke with President William Ruto about the implications of the 2024 bilateral migration and mobility partnership and more opportunities for language and vocational training.

There are now around 9,500 Kenyans working in Germany, and nearly 1,300 in vocational training. "We want to open up opportunities for young people and create regular, fair and orderly pathways for labor and skilled worker migration," Steinmeier said in Nairobi.

German SMEs also interested in Africa

Vocational training is said to be most effective where businesses and factories are being established.

"A very favorable window of opportunity for investment is currently opening up in Africa," said Fritz Audebert, CEO of ICUnet, a company that advises German firms on investment projects worldwide. "We've noticed a shift over the past two years or so, driven in part by geopolitical changes, the complicated situation in China, and most recently the war in Iran."

"More and more companies are beginning to understand this," Audebert added. "While there are reservations, we're seeing a similar sentiment to that regarding India." What's new is that small and medium-sized enterprises from Germany are also showing interest in Africa.

During the trip, Audebert was particularly impressed by Cote d'Ivoire, as he said, "because of the ministers' high level of expertise." The country is the world's largest cocoa exporter and possesses important raw materials. "You can work well with this potential," he said.

Opportunities for German automakers in Africa?

Members of the business delegation accompanying Steinmeier also agreed that the German automotive industry must focus more on the African market.

"The middle class is growing in cities, and with it, the demand for mobility," said Audebert.

Markus Thill, president of Bosch Africa, confirms there is a considerable market for simple, gas- and diesel-driven cars. "Based on the auto industry's experience, we know that households worldwide with an annual income of €10,000 or more can afford a new car," said Thill. This would mean that potentially 5-10 million new cars per year could be built and sold in Africa.

Instead, "we export millions of old used cars to Africa that would no longer be eligible for registration in Europe," he said.

Not just business: African nations as political partners

Even though the focus of the trip was on the economy, "we shouldn't limit our view to that," Steinmeier said at the end of his trip. Germany maintains a reliable political partnership with Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana and Kenya.

"These are three countries with which we cooperate closely on the international stage, and in that sense, visiting them now was the right and deliberate choice," he said.

When asked to take stock of his 30 trips to African countries undertaken during his political career, Steinmeier said: "There is not one Africa, but many, and there are also very different, uneven developments there." This fact, he concluded, needs to be "communicated even more effectively" in Germany.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Trump says he urged Putin to 'pull back' military aggression in Europe
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump claimed that he talked with Vladimir Putin about ceasing Russia's military aggression in Europe and expressed his belief in the possibility of a deal between Russia and Ukraine.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump says he urged Putin to 'pull back' military aggression in Europe

November 26, 2026

US President Donald Trump claimed that he talked with Vladimir Putin about ceasing Russia's military aggression in Europe and expressed his belief in the possibility of a deal between Russia and Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that he had urged his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to cease "military aggression" in Europe during their talks in China.

"I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly," Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.

However, the US president did not specify which European territories he mentioned when communicating with Putin. This week, Poland — a NATO member — accused Russia of deliberately violating its airspace.

Trump added that he believes there is a "strong possibility" of such a deal between Russia and Ukraine. "Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH," he wrote in the post.

Trump and Rutte call for 'peaceful resolution'

Trump's post on Truth Social came a day after he hosted NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Florida. They issued a joint statement afterward calling on Russia not to expand the war in Ukraine.

"We also talked about, at length, the importance of Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the War — and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the War, as rapidly as possible," the statement said.

Trump's comments represent a shift in tone after he cordially called Putin a friend during their meeting in China last week. Approaching Putin, smiling Trump said, "Who is he? He's my friend." Then he shook hands warmly with the Russian leader.

The echoes of the scene reverberated throughout Ukraine and other European nations, which are worried that Trump might side with Putin.

The US president had said he could end the war in Ukraine on the first day of his second term in office.

Russian refinery on fire after attack

Depite Trump's comments, the war shows no signs of ending, with both Russia and Ukraine continuing their mutual attacks.

A fire broke out on Thursday at the Slavyansk ECO oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region following a drone attack. The strike caused serious damage, according to a social media post by the company.

According to Reuters, two industry sources estimated that Ukrainian drone attacks have reduced the combined crude processing volumes of Russian oil refineries by 45% since late October.

At the same time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that Russia is preparing for a large-scale attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, logistics, and essential services.

Zelenskyy also said that crews are working to restore electricity in six Ukrainian regions after Russia launched ballistic missiles and 113 drones overnight.

entries.title: Protests in Iraqi Kurdistan at plans for government in Baghdad to take over oil, border crossings
entries.summary: Thousands have gathered in the capital of northern Iraq's semiautonomous Kurdish region, waving flags and voicing opposition to plans for the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings.
entries.content:
Iraq

Mass protests in Kurdish Irbil against Iraqi government reform plans

November 26, 2026

Thousands have gathered in the capital of northern Iraq's semiautonomous Kurdish region, waving flags and voicing opposition to plans for the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings.

Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq. 

They were responding to federal government plans announced earlier in the week for Baghdad to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities. 

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had said the measures were part of a bid to stop oil smuggling when announcing the changes.

According to state media reports, later on Thursday, Iraqi border forces closed two border crossings with Syria and Iran that had been administered by the Kurdish authorities.

Iraq's border forces commander told the Iraqi News Agency that the al-Waleed border crossing with Syria and the Bashta border crossing with Iran have been closed.

Rival Kurdish factions unite to protest plans

The plans marked an escalation in the long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities that have largely governed themselves since 1991, albeit with varying levels of recognition and authority.

Rival Kurdish parties joined forces for the large protests in the regional capital.

Protests were also reported to have spread to several other towns and cities beyond the capital.

Iraq's 2005 constitution, written following the US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, formally recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But authorities in Erbil and Baghdad have remained in a tug of war over the control of land, oil and money ever since.

Tuesday's decision, which received backing from Iraq's Federal Supreme Court a day later, brings border crossing in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in four contested provinces — Kirkuk, Diyala, Salahuddin and Nineveh.

The Kurdish regional government's Cabinet said on Wednesday that the decision from Baghdad "violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan region," saying it represented "an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime."

Prime Minister al-Zaidi, who took office earlier this year with the backing of US President Donald Trump, also dismissed Kirkuk's operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He said the measures reflected Iraq's "independent national will."

Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said his government was "surprised" by al-Zaidi's decisions and called them "completely unacceptable."

Contested region even since 2005 reformation

Iraq's Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the authority of the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) only covered the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the US-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein.

Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week's orders.

The 2005 constitution tried to solve the fate of some of the disputed territories in the lands between the borders to Syria and Iran that are home to a host of ethnicities and communities but with Kurds generally the majority group.

Article 140 called for reversing Saddam-era policies of expelling Kurds and moving Arabs in, and called for a census and a referendum on whether the disputed regions should join the Kurdistan region. Neither was held.

Kurdish forces then gained more of the disputed territory after Iraqi forces were forced out by the so-called "Islamic State," with Kurdish pershmerga for subsequently reclaiming some of the land with some international assistance.

The oil-rich region is highly important to both administrations, in a country that relies on oil revenues for the vast majority of its public sector budget.

Internal political tensions within Iraqi Kurdistan have further complicated the issue in recent months, with the Federal Supreme Court hearing an ongoing challenge against the current government's legitimacy after a party withdrew from the coalition cabinet. But rival Kurdish political factions seem to have found common ground on this issue at least.

entries.title: Germany: IG Metall union says deal reached with employers
entries.summary: IG Metall, representing millions of workers in Germany's metal and electrical industry, is the country's largest trade union. The deal came after more than 24 hours of talks with employers.
entries.content:
November 26, 2026

IG Metall, representing millions of workers in Germany's metal and electrical industry, is the country's largest trade union. The deal came after more than 24 hours of talks with employers.

Germany's powerful IG Metall trade union said Thursday it has reached a pay deal with employers after more than 24 hours of the fourth round of talks.

What is in the deal?

IG Metall and employers agreed on the following points in their agreement:

  • The deal foresees a pay increase in two phases: 2.0% from May 2027 and 2.3% from April 2028
  • The agreement will also entail one-off payments in March 2027 of between €150 ($164) and €450
  • The collective agreements will be in effect until November 30, 2028
  • Companies will be allowed to deviate from the 35-hour work week in talks with employees
  • Firms will also be allowed to ask employees to give up pay to help finance investments
  • The agreements will cover the 1.7 million workers represented by IG Metall in the German states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Baden-Württemberg
  • The deal will also ensure new investments and jobs in Germany with companies making binding commitments

What is IG Metal and what are the significance of the talks?

IG Metall represents 3.7 million workers in the German metal and electrical industry in total. It is Germany's largest trade union. 

"The result is a compromise under difficult conditions," Baden-Württemberg IG Metall boss Barbara Resch said.

The talks come amid job cuts across multiple sectors in the German economy, such as the automotive sector.

IG Metall represents workers in major German companies such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Siemens, ThyssenKrupp, and Salzgitter AG, among others. All of those aforementioned companies have announced job-cutting plans within the last two years. 

German companies are attempting to slash labor costs and cut benefits as the German economy faces increasing competition from China and pressure from US tariffs. This also means that labor unions are being presented with less desirable packages for employees.
